title: The Lens Factory Fred Hollows Planned for Eritrea and Never Saw
dek: Already diagnosed with cancer, the eye surgeon Fred Hollows set out in 1990 to make cataract lenses in Eritrea instead of importing them.

story.event: Deciding, after a cancer diagnosis, to build an intraocular lens factory in Eritrea and raising the money for it
story.summary: On a second visit to war-torn Eritrea in 1990, after being diagnosed with metastatic kidney cancer, the ophthalmologist Fred Hollows conceived a factory to make intraocular lenses locally, which he estimated would cut their cost from about $150 to $2. He raised money in Australia, the Australian government funded equipment assembled in Wollongong, and in 1992 he set up the Fred Hollows Foundation. He died in February 1993; the Asmara factory opened in 1994.
paragraphs: In 1987 Fred Hollows, a New Zealand-born eye surgeon who had worked at the University of New South Wales since 1965, made his first trip to Eritrea, then fighting a war of independence against Ethiopia. The visit was arranged by Fessehaie Abraham, an Eritrean refugee in Sydney who had first met Hollows in 1980 as a trachoma patient and handed him a pamphlet about his country's cause. Hollows came home impressed, the Australian Dictionary of Biography records, by the underground hospital and the medical manufacturing plants that Eritreans were running in wartime.

What he knew was mostly arithmetic. Surveying eye health for the World Health Organization, he had found that most blindness in poor countries was preventable and that cataract was its commonest cause. The operation needed an intraocular lens, and Western makers charged $150 or more for one, a price people in Eritrea or Nepal could not pay. He also knew, from 1989, that he had metastatic kidney cancer. "I could see no reason why they couldn't manufacture intra-ocular lenses," he wrote in his autobiography.

In 1990, already ill, he went back to Eritrea with a 60 Minutes crew and came away with the idea of a lens factory there. He calculated, Stephen Howes of the Development Policy Centre later wrote, that it would cut the cost of a lens from $150 to $2. It was his first large fundraising effort in Australia. The Australian government paid for a factory to be assembled in Wollongong and shipped to Eritrea, Prime Minister Paul Keating's office noted in 1993, and Hollows began raising money for others, including one in Nepal planned with the surgeon Sanduk Ruit. In September 1992 he, his wife Gabi and close friends set up the Fred Hollows Foundation so the work would outlast him.

He did not see the factories run. Hollows died at home in Sydney on 10 February 1993. The Asmara factory was opened in 1994 by Australia's foreign minister, Gareth Evans, and the Nepal laboratory also began production after his death. By 2017, Howes reported, the Eritrean factory had made 2.2 million lenses; the Foundation says the price of a lens fell from more than A$150 to less than A$5.

quote.text: Be generous to the extent of thy power. If thou hast not dug a well in the desert, at least place a lamp in a shrine.
quote.locator: Chapter II, Concerning Benevolence, 'Story of a Man and a Thirsty Dog'
quote.source_title: The Bustān of Sadi, tr. A. Hart Edwards, Project Gutenberg eBook #60471
quote.connection: Hollows dug the well: a factory in a country at war, begun when he knew he was ill. Saadi asks something smaller of most people and does not count it as less, measuring generosity against what is in your power rather than against anyone else's.

reflection: Hollows had a short list of facts and a short amount of time: lenses cost too much, Eritreans were already making medical supplies in wartime, and his cancer was not going away. He did not need to see the factory open to know it was worth starting.

Most work is not on that scale, and it does not need to be. Saadi measures generosity against what is in your power, and some days your power is small: a long shift, a tired body, a family that needs you home. On those days the lamp counts. So does setting up what you begin so that someone else could finish it.
invitation: Choose one piece of work you have started that someone else may one day need to carry on. Write a short note today saying where it stands and what the next step would be.

cross_checks.claim: Hollows first visited Eritrea in 1987, during its war of independence.
Imported intraocular lenses cost about $150 or more, beyond what patients in Eritrea and Nepal could pay.
The Australian government funded the Eritrean lens factory, built in Australia and shipped to Eritrea.
Hollows founded the Foundation in 1992 and died on 10 February 1993, before the factories opened.

research_notes: Region and country follow the editor's note: the episode is set in Eritrea (East Africa), though the fundraising and the Foundation were in Australia. Lens prices disagree. Hollows's own estimate, reported by Howes, was $150 down to $2 a lens; the Foundation's history says the cost fell from more than A$150 to less than A$5; the Encyclopedia of Australian Science says the factories cut the cost by around 70 per cent; another Foundation page gives US$200 for imported lenses. The story gives Hollows's estimate as his own calculation and the Foundation's figure as the Foundation's, and says only 'more than $150' for the imported price. Opening dates: Howes, the Australian of the Year citation and the Foundation say 1994; the ADB says only that the Nepal, Eritrea and Vietnam factories started production after his death; some accounts date the Nepal laboratory to 1995, so the story gives no year for Nepal. Output: Howes (2017) gives 2.2 million lenses from Asmara; the Foundation (2025) gives about 250,000 a year and more than eight million since opening for its laboratories combined; the story uses Howes's attributed figure. The Hollows quotation is from his autobiography with Peter Corris, as quoted in the ADB (the ADB's quotation continues after an ellipsis, which is not used). The ADB is cited from an Internet Archive copy because adb.anu.edu.au refuses automated requests. Funding: the factory was paid for with Australian government money and public donations and run as a non-profit; 'nonprofit' is used. The Saadi lines come from a passage on benevolence and are followed in the source by a footnote marker, which is omitted.
